The paper applies frequency domain methods to electromagnetic transient analysis of very large multi-phase power distribution networks.
Network elements modeled include lumped and distributed parameter lines, transformers, circuit breakers, sources, and loads.
Frequency domain modeling avoids rational fitting approximations required in time domain solutions.
Kron’s reduction is used to reduce the system admittance matrix by eliminating nodes not of interest.
The Numerical Laplace Transform (NLT) is employed for numerical inversion from frequency to time domain.
Circuit breakers are modeled using Norton equivalent circuits and superposition principle for switching transitions.
The method is verified against ATP/EMTP simulations on IEEE 13-bus and 34-bus feeders showing excellent agreement.
Further testing on IEEE 123-bus and a synthetic 1188-node system confirms accuracy and computational efficiency.
The FD method captures both symmetrical and unsymmetrical fault transients accurately.
Initial steady-state conditions are incorporated by calculating phasor voltages and transforming to the Laplace domain.
The admittance matrix is constructed by assembling admittance models of individual components using multiphase nodal analysis.
Distributed parameter line models use Telegrapher's equations in the Laplace domain with modal decomposition.
Transformer models include single-phase and three-phase configurations with magnetization branches in the frequency domain.
The method supports various transformer winding connections including delta-wye grounded configurations.
The FD approach offers substantial computational savings compared to time domain tools, enabling large-scale EMT studies.
The Numerical Laplace Transform uses odd frequency sampling and window functions to reduce truncation errors.
The method can simulate multiple circuit breaker operations sequentially using superposition.
The system matrix size and solution time are benchmarked to demonstrate the effectiveness of network reduction.
The method is flexible and adaptable for utility companies and engineering firms for system-wide transient assessments.
The paper provides detailed modeling guidelines for common power system components in the frequency domain.
